subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Ecosystems and Food Webs
subtitle: Life science revision pack on ecosystems, food webs, energy flow, matter cycling, biodiversity, and ecosystem change.
description: This pack helps students revise how living and nonliving parts interact in ecosystems. It covers producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains, food webs, energy flow, matter cycling, biodiversity, population change, human impacts, data interpretation, and fair-test investigation skills.

data.targetWord: a system made of living and nonliving parts interacting in an area

examples.en-US: A pond with fish, algae, water, mud, sunlight, and bacteria is an ecosystem.

data.targetWord: a group of parts that interact and work together

examples.en-US: A forest ecosystem is a system because its parts affect one another.

data.targetWord: a living or once-living part of an ecosystem

examples.en-US: Trees, insects, bacteria, dead leaves, and animal waste are biotic factors.

data.targetWord: a nonliving part of an ecosystem

examples.en-US: Sunlight, water, air, rocks, soil minerals, wind, and temperature are abiotic factors.

data.targetWord: one individual living thing

examples.en-US: One rabbit, one oak tree, or one mushroom is an organism.

data.targetWord: a group of similar organisms that can reproduce with each other

examples.en-US: Gray wolves, honeybees, and red maple trees are examples of species.

data.targetWord: all members of one species living in the same area

examples.en-US: All frogs living in one pond form a frog population.

data.targetWord: all the different populations living and interacting in an area

examples.en-US: Frogs, fish, algae, insects, and bacteria in a pond form a community.

data.targetWord: the place where an organism lives and gets what it needs

examples.en-US: A desert can be the habitat of a cactus.

data.targetWord: the role an organism has in its ecosystem

examples.en-US: A bee has a niche that includes pollinating flowers and feeding on nectar.

data.targetWord: an organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis

examples.en-US: Grass, algae, trees, and clover are producers.

data.targetWord: an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms

examples.en-US: Deer, wolves, grasshoppers, and humans are consumers.

data.targetWord: a consumer that eats producers

examples.en-US: A rabbit eating grass is a primary consumer.

data.targetWord: a consumer that eats primary consumers

examples.en-US: A frog that eats a grasshopper is a secondary consumer.

data.targetWord: a higher-level consumer that eats secondary consumers

examples.en-US: A hawk that eats a snake can be a tertiary consumer.

data.targetWord: a consumer that eats plants or algae

examples.en-US: A deer, rabbit, caterpillar, or sea urchin is a herbivore.

data.targetWord: a consumer that eats animals

examples.en-US: A hawk, shark, snake, or fox is a carnivore.

data.targetWord: a consumer that eats both plants and animals

examples.en-US: A bear or human is an omnivore.

data.targetWord: an organism that breaks down dead organisms and waste

examples.en-US: Fungi and bacteria are decomposers that recycle matter.

data.targetWord: an organism that eats dead material or pieces of waste

examples.en-US: Earthworms and millipedes are detritivores.

data.targetWord: a simple model showing one path of energy flow

examples.en-US: Grass to grasshopper to frog to snake to hawk is a food chain.

data.targetWord: a model showing many connected food chains in an ecosystem

examples.en-US: A meadow food web can connect grass, mice, snakes, birds, foxes, and hawks.

data.targetWord: the ability to cause change or do work

examples.en-US: Sunlight energy helps plants make sugar.

data.targetWord: anything that has mass and takes up space

examples.en-US: Water, carbon dioxide, oxygen, sugar, and minerals are matter.

data.targetWord: the process producers use to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water using light energy

examples.en-US: Plants and algae use photosynthesis to store energy in sugar.

data.targetWord: an organism that hunts and eats another organism

examples.en-US: An owl hunting a mouse is a predator.

data.targetWord: an organism that is hunted and eaten

examples.en-US: A mouse eaten by an owl is prey.

data.targetWord: a struggle between organisms for the same limited resource

examples.en-US: Two plants may compete for sunlight, water, and space.

data.targetWord: a relationship where both organisms benefit

examples.en-US: A bee gets nectar while a flower gets pollinated.

data.targetWord: a relationship where one organism benefits and the other is not helped or harmed much

examples.en-US: A bird nesting in a tree is a common example of commensalism.

data.targetWord: a relationship where one organism benefits and the other is harmed

examples.en-US: A tick feeding on a deer is parasitism.

data.targetWord: the variety of living things in an ecosystem

examples.en-US: A coral reef or diverse prairie has high biodiversity.

data.targetWord: the ability of a system to keep functioning when conditions change

examples.en-US: A diverse prairie may recover after a drought because it has stability.

data.targetWord: the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance

examples.en-US: High biodiversity can improve ecosystem resilience.

data.targetWord: a resource or condition that restricts population growth

examples.en-US: Food, water, space, shelter, disease, and predators can be limiting factors.

data.targetWord: a testable explanation or prediction

examples.en-US: If more light increases plant growth, then plants in more light will grow taller is a hypothesis.

data.targetWord: the factor changed by the scientist in an investigation

examples.en-US: Hours of light is the independent variable in an algae growth test.

data.targetWord: the factor measured in an investigation

examples.en-US: Plant height is a dependent variable when testing fertilizer.

data.targetWord: a factor kept the same to make an investigation fair

examples.en-US: Plant species, soil type, container size, and water amount can be controlled variables.

data.targetWord: data or observations used to support a claim

examples.en-US: A table showing plant growth over time is evidence.

data.targetWord: rapid algae growth, often caused by extra nutrients in water

examples.en-US: Fertilizer runoff can cause an algal bloom in a lake.

data.targetWord: a change at one feeding level that affects other levels in a food web

examples.en-US: Fewer sea otters can lead to more sea urchins and less kelp in a trophic cascade.

data.targetWord: a species introduced to a new area that may cause harm

examples.en-US: A new fish with no major predators may compete with native fish.

data.targetWord: fertilizer washed from land into water by rain

examples.en-US: Fertilizer runoff can add nitrogen and phosphorus to lakes.

data.targetWord: oxygen mixed into water that aquatic animals need to survive

examples.en-US: Fish may die if dissolved oxygen drops too low.

data.title: Levels of Organization in an Ecosystem
data.instruction: Put the organization levels from smallest to largest.
items: One organism, such as one frog.
A population, such as all frogs in one pond.
A community, such as frogs, fish, insects, algae, and bacteria.
An ecosystem, including the community plus water, sunlight, mud, oxygen, and temperature.

data.title: Energy Flow Through a Food Chain
data.instruction: Put the energy-flow steps in the most common order.
items: Sunlight provides energy for most ecosystems.
Producers capture light energy and make sugar.
Primary consumers eat producers.
Secondary consumers eat primary consumers.
Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
Decomposers break down dead material from all levels.

data.title: Matter Cycling in an Ecosystem
data.instruction: Put the matter-cycling steps in order.
items: A tree takes in carbon dioxide from the air.
The tree uses carbon atoms to build sugars and wood.
A caterpillar eats a leaf from the tree.
A bird eats the caterpillar.
Waste and dead organisms are broken down by decomposers.
Matter returns to soil, water, or air.
Plants use some of the matter again.

data.title: Fertilizer Runoff and Fish Deaths
data.instruction: Put the cause-and-effect chain in order.
items: Rain washes fertilizer from lawns or farms into a lake.
Extra nutrients enter the water.
Algae grow rapidly and form an algal bloom.
Large amounts of algae die.
Decomposers break down the dead algae and use oxygen.
Dissolved oxygen decreases.
Fish and other aquatic animals may die.

data.title: Predator-Prey Population Pattern
data.instruction: Put the common predator-prey pattern in order.
items: A prey population increases.
Predators have more food available.
The predator population later increases.
Predators eat more prey.
The prey population decreases.
Predators then have less food and may decrease.
